verification.note: Publisher description checked: oral and written materials, reconstructed edition prepared by Obadiah after the original manuscript was lost, and original 1921 publication. Full book unread; the modern reprint and publisher’s priority language are not substitutes for assessing its particular historical claims.

verification.note: Selected primary historiographical passages, Fage pp. 38–41 and Curtin pp. 64–65, read for older African writing and differing institutional settings. Their evaluative judgments and sweeping priority claims are not adopted. Specific university founding dates in this retrospective require independent checking and are not imported.

strand.title: Critical study of transmitted traditions
strand.focus: Transmission, genre and social context demand interpretation, distinct from collecting eyewitness interviews.

source_context.title: Jan Vansina, “Oral Tradition and Its Methodology,” in General History of Africa I (1981): 142–165.

verification.note: Primary pp. 142–144 read: intergenerational transmission, literary form, social context and distinction from eyewitness testimony. This chapter is not the 1985 book. Its claim that valid traditions ultimately require eyewitness foundations is an authorial methodological position, not an undisputed rule.

source_context.title: Jan Vansina, Oral Tradition as History (University of Wisconsin Press, 1985).

verification.note: Publisher search listing checked for the 1985 book and its relationship to the 1961 work; full publisher page was unavailable. Not evidence for all African historiography.

strand.title: Spoken knowledge and its custodians

source_context.title: Amadou Hampâté Bâ, “The Living Tradition,” in General History of Africa I (1981): 166–205.

verification.note: Primary pp. 166–168 read. The author explicitly restricts his direct examples to savannah traditions south of the Sahara that he knows, especially former French West Africa. His situated account of spoken knowledge and transmission is not a single essence of all African societies; full chapter unread.

verification.note: HRAF scholarly abstract and metadata checked: Nnobi fieldwork in 1980–82 and historical comparison of women’s positions before, during and after colonial rule. strand.title: Mombasa: collective action and differentiated reform
strand.focus: Cooper’s 1947 case links neighborhood coordination, varied occupations and rural provisioning to strike solidarity. Differentiated wage gains and repression then weakened the African Workers’ Federation. The resulting stabilization programme was an official response, not simply the strikers’ demand.

strand.title: African histories within diaspora reconstruction
strand.focus: Lovejoy proposes connecting diaspora research to historically specific African backgrounds and individual trajectories. This is a scoped programme, not timeless ethnic continuity or a claim that all diaspora scholarship adopts it.

source_context.scope_note: Indexed author abstract read from university-hosted article. Supports a specific African-centred diaspora research programme. Full PDF retrieval failed certificate verification; no body or reception claim.

strand.title: Founding exchange and historical problems
strand.focus: The 1929 editors invite exchanges across specialties, without claiming to invent economic/social history. Belief and culture are present from the outset.

verification.note: Complete short English translation read; original metadata checked at https://www.persee.fr/doc/ahess_0003-441x_1929_num_1_1_1031 . Founders acknowledge predecessors, legitimate specialties and the need to exchange results across disciplinary and past/present divisions. This is a programmatic statement, not proof that all subsequent work achieved its aspirations.

source_context.title: Marc Bloch, The Royal Touch: Sacred Monarchy and Scrofula in England and France, translated by J. E. Anderson (1973); Routledge reissue 2015.

verification.note: Indexed publisher description and JSTOR publisher table of contents checked: supernatural attributes of royal power and comparative French/English healing ritual, with a critical interpretation section. source_context.title: Lucien Febvre: The Problem of Unbelief

verification.note: Google Books publisher description read: French original 1942, English Harvard edition 1982; polemic against treating Rabelais as a covert modern atheist and investigation of historically available ideas/beliefs. This is a description, not a primary-book reading. Walker’s separate 1983 review supplies criticism and personal reception; the claim that unbelief was universally impossible is not adopted.

strand.title: Braudel’s multiple historical times
strand.focus: Models must survive comparison with changing evidence; their failure matters. Braudel’s productive Lévi-Strauss borrowing and Chartier’s later objection to an explanatory hierarchy mark disagreements within this conversation.

source_context.title: Fernand Braudel, “Histoire et sciences sociales: La longue durée” (1958), reprinted in Réseaux 5, no. 27 (1987): 7–37. DOI 10.3406/reso.1987.1320.

verification.note: Cached PDF text consulted: reprint header, opening disciplinary exchange, pp. 24–25 mechanical/statistical models and pp. 28–31 Lévi-Strauss discussion. Braudel explicitly borrows a model distinction, appreciates structural anthropology and insists on models’ historical lifespans, breakdown and testing; Spooner’s monetary collaboration supplies an example. Original 1958 printing not collated. Direct download returned 404; cached text was available, screenshots were not. These are selected primary passages, not a full-book check.

source_context.title: Roger Chartier: representations and social practices

verification.note: Full primary article pp. 1505–1520 read from the scan, using OCR. These are Chartier’s arguments and attributed receptions, not independent verification of every historical example.

strand.title: Traces, questions and comparative reasoning
strand.focus: Bloch distinguishes deliberate from unintended testimony and origins from causes. Present observation can inform questions, without making past and present identical.

source_context.title: Marc Bloch, Apologie pour l’histoire ou Métier d’historien (first published 1949); consulted second edition, 1952.

verification.note: Selected primary PDF pages 19–20, 27–29, 34 and 37–39 read: origins versus explanation; Pirenne and present observation; Maitland and regressive inquiry; Simiand’s knowledge by traces; intentional/unintentional testimony and limits on knowledge. The 1941 heading is not publication date. These methodological passages do not verify every example or the whole unfinished book. Later causal discussion and original manuscript not read.

strand.title: Historical psychology and its criticisms
strand.focus: Febvre historicizes collective feelings with psychological resources and a critical Huizinga reading. Walker later questions universal claims about what people could think.
strand.works: “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941); The Problem of Unbelief (1942); Walker review (1983)

verification.note: Primary preface PDF pp. 10–11 and selected 1941 essay passages at PDF pp. 261–269 and 276–278 read. Foreword names Reclus, Burckhardt, Berr and other resources; essay credits Wallon and Blondel, appreciates and questions Huizinga, and proposes differentiated evidence for collective feelings. Its evolutionary psychological language is not adopted. EPHE bibliography confirms the collection’s original publication in 1953 despite the UQAM page’s 1952 heading; consulted edition is 1992. Full collection and original 1941 printing not collated.

source_context.title: D. P. Walker, “Which Side Was Rabelais On?”, The New York Review of Books, 31 March 1983.

verification.note: Review text read. Walker credits the book’s formative effect on his teaching and research while disputing the universal impossibility of anti-Christian thought and criticizing primitive-mentality assumptions. He distinguishes Lefranc polemic, Busson counterexamples and later scholarship. This is a contemporary scholar’s situated assessment and direct reception testimony, not independent checking of every sixteenth-century example.

strand.title: Village reconstruction and mediated voices

strand.title: Models and the critical turn

strand.title: Historical particularism and comparison
strand.focus: Comparable appearances do not establish common causes; investigate particular histories before generalizing.

strand.title: Relations and transformations
strand.focus: A qualified adaptation of phonology; structural explanation still uses history.

strand.title: Social facts and institutional resistance
strand.focus: Durkheim’s examples include obligations, signs and monetary practices. Externality and coercive capacity distinguish his object; mere statistical commonness does not suffice.

source_context.title: Émile Durkheim, Les Règles de la méthode sociologique (1895); consulted Alcan edition, 1919, chapters I and V.

verification.note: Primary chapter I opening and later definition passages, and chapter V opening read in the linked Wikisource chapters. Social facts include signs, obligations and institutions with externality and resistance; common occurrence alone is insufficient. Chapter V explicitly criticizes Comte and Spencer for conflating utility with origins and distinguishes causes from functions, including survivals and changed uses. The later printing is identified; no complete comparative-method or original-edition collation claimed.

strand.title: Origins, functions and critical antecedents

strand.title: Differentiation and failures of solidarity
strand.focus: Division of labor can produce conflict and anomie. Durkheim’s discussion of crises and capital/labor antagonism qualifies any automatic equation of differentiation with cohesion.

verification.note: Primary opening of the chapter on anomic division read. Durkheim discusses crises and capital/labor antagonism as failures of solidarity; differentiation does not guarantee integration. The normal/pathological vocabulary and his historical examples are his claims, not independently verified conclusions. Full book and chapter on forced division remain unread here.

strand.title: Religious life and collective categories
strand.focus: Sacred practices and collective membership are distinguished from a purely private belief. The proposed social formation of categories is an argument to assess, not an established origin of all thought.
strand.works: Elementary Forms (1912), introduction and religion definition

source_context.title: Émile Durkheim, Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse (1912); The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life, translated by Joseph Ward Swain (1915).

verification.note: Primary selected introduction pp. 9–19, religion definition pp. 46–47, and conclusion IV on categories read in Gutenberg transcription. Supports the proposed social formation of categories and collective practices around sacred things. Durkheim presents a sociological alternative to individual empiricism and unexplained apriorism. Australian ethnographic evidence and claims about earliest religion are not independently established by these readings; the book is not treated as a current ethnographic authority.

strand.title: Sacrifice, participants and mediation
strand.focus: Hubert and Mauss build on and revise earlier comparative scholarship. Their provisional model distinguishes ritual participants and movement between sacred and profane.
strand.works: “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

verification.note: Primary introduction, selected definitional passages and conclusion on mediation read in the 1909 reprint. The authors acknowledge Tylor, Robertson Smith and Frazer while proposing a different, explicitly provisional theory; they distinguish participants and ritual movement between sacred and profane. UQAM catalogue confirms original L’Année sociologique 2 (1899), 29–138: https://classiques.uqam.ca/classiques/mauss_marcel/oeuvres_1/oeuvres_1_3/essai_sacrifice.html . Detailed Sanskrit/Hebrew cases not independently checked.

Remaining pages, including the famous three-idols passage, not read here; editorial reception is not attributed to Simiand himself.

source_context.title: Friedrich Wilhelm Graf, “Weber, Marianne, geborene Schnitger,” Neue Deutsche Biographie 27 (2020), 477–479.

verification.note: Read biography paragraphs and works list, including the 1900 Fichte/Marx study, 1907 legal-history project and posthumous editions/1926 biography of Max Weber. This is a scholarly secondary account, not reading her original books. Supports intellectual authorship, situated feminist legal criticism and editorial mediation; do not reduce her role to marriage or presume agreement with every position held by her husband.

source_context.title: Stanford Encyclopedia: Max Weber

verification.note: Read sections 1, 2, 3 and 4.1 completely; only opening of 4.2, not sections 5–6. Supports the historical-economics milieu/Schmoller commission, selective Rickert reception, Marianne’s editorial role and disputed unity of posthumous Economy and Society. This is a scholarly interpretation; questionable incidental chronology and evaluative political phrasing are not adopted.

strand.title: Different comparative and institutional receptions
strand.focus: Parsons’s translation and institutional comparison, Lipset’s democracy analysis and Bendix’s authority/citizenship inquiry select different resources. No single modernization reading exhausts Weber.

source_context.title: Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, translated by Talcott Parsons (1930), Routledge 2001 edition: translator’s preface and conclusion.

verification.note: Read title/imprint/contents, complete Parsons preface xxv–xxvii and printed 119–125 (chapter V conclusion) in the 2001 reissue/electronic 2005 witness. Parsons translates the 1920 revision of the 1904–05 essay; the separate author introduction belongs to the 1920 collected religion studies, not the original essay. Weber rejects replacing one-sided materialism with one-sided spiritualism and leaves future outcomes open. Notes 97–119, other body pages, German and original essay versions uncollated.

source_context.title: Lipset: social requisites of democracy (1959)

verification.note: Earlier journal metadata check expanded to primary scanned title/source page and printed 69–71, 84–87, 102–104, read using local OCR. Democracy definitions cite Schumpeter/Weber; legitimacy differs from effectiveness; conclusion explicitly rejects guaranteed democratization and uses Weber via Richard Pipes. Appendix p. 104 cites Lazarsfeld for multivariate analysis while retaining ideal types as another useful method. Other pages, including final appendix p. 105, unread; no independent replication of classifications/statistics.

source_context.title: Reinhard Bendix, Nation-Building and Citizenship: Studies of Our Changing Social Order (Wiley, 1964; enlarged editions 1977 and 1996).

verification.note: Publisher description checked for authority, citizenship and comparisons across Europe, Russia, Japan and India; original Wiley 1964 metadata corroborated by Stewart Library https://libcat.weber.edu/bib/895564 . The linked 1996 edition includes John Bendix’s introduction; he is not coauthor of the original. Publisher biography at https://www.routledge.com/From-Berlin-to-Berkeley-German-Jewish-Identities/Bendix/p/book/9781041303480 explicitly documents Reinhard’s Weber engagement. No full text read, and additions to enlarged editions are not silently dated 1964.

source_context.title: Parsons: evolutionary universals (1964)

verification.note: Earlier university abstract check retained; now read primary JSTOR title leaf and printed 339–341, 348–350, 355–357 at https://sethabrutyn.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/parsons-talcott_evolutionary-universals-in-society.pdf . Explicit Durkheim Elementary Forms resource p. 341, Weber bureaucracy pp. 348–349, Smelser/Eisenstadt resources and Harvard seminar acknowledgment of Bellah/Eisenstadt p. 339. Evolutionary claims and communist-future predictions remain attributed, not confirmed. Pages 342–347 and 351–354 unread.

strand.title: Earlier histories of work and their disagreements
strand.focus: Clark’s overlapping household forms and Pinchbeck’s industrial transition ask different period questions. Paid and unpaid production, training, marital status and class complicate a single progress/decline story; maternalist commitments remain visible.

source_context.title: Alice Clark, Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919), preface, introduction and conclusion.

verification.note: Complete preface, introduction pp. 1–13 and conclusion pp. 290–308 read. Credits Schreiner, Knowles and Power’s unpublished material; distinguishes overlapping production forms, class and marital position, and paid/unpaid work. Acknowledges conjectural medieval comparisons and tentative causal conclusions. Maternal, racial and civilizational assumptions are historical commitments, not adopted facts. Main occupational chapters unread; quoted Pepys material in conclusion is mediated by Clark.

source_context.title: Ivy Pinchbeck: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution

verification.note: Additional publisher-preview reading: complete original preface vi, complete introduction pp. 1–5, 1969 reprint preface signed October 1968, and opening chapter I p. 7. Distinguishes occupational visibility, family wages, training, marital status, disruption and claimed eventual gains. Names Knowles, Power, scholarship support and George. The later preface proposes post-1850 research rather than supplying it. Remaining occupational chapters and conclusion unread; optimistic generalization is attributed, not independently proven. Previous scope: Publisher-distributed preview: copyright page confirms 1930 original and 1969 reprint; original preface p. vi acknowledges Eileen Power’s research direction and Lilian Knowles’s earlier guidance; introduction pp. 1–2 addresses women’s work before industrialization. Full book and later reception not audited.

strand.title: Documents, rights and historical agency
strand.focus: Beard’s documentary project, Spruill’s colonial study and Flexner’s rights history offer different forms of recovery.
strand.works: Woman as Force in History (1946); Women’s Life and Work (1938); Century of Struggle (1959)

source_context.title: Mary Ritter Beard: Woman as Force in History

verification.note: Archival description checked for the 1946 work and its argument for women’s active historical contributions; not a complete appraisal of Beard’s claims.

source_context.title: Mary Ritter Beard and women’s documentary collections

verification.note: Institutional account connects Beard and Margaret Storrs Grierson to the collection’s 1942 founding. Supports documentary institution-building, not sole authorship of the whole archive.

source_context.title: Julia Cherry Spruill: Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies

verification.note: Norton description checked for original publication in 1938, documentary subject matter, and Scott’s role in later republication. The 1998 listing is a reissue; the book’s treatment of race and class still needs close reading.

source_context.title: Eleanor Flexner: Century of Struggle

verification.note: Swarthmore catalogue identifies the 1996 edition. “1930” beside Flexner’s name is her graduating class, not the publication year. The 1959 original is corroborated by the contemporary review record DOI 10.1177/000271626032800132; publisher full text was unavailable.

strand.title: Socialist and feminist historical work
strand.focus: Class, community and women’s organizing are connected questions, with differences among practitioners.
strand.works: Outsiders (1993); Hidden from History (1973); Eve and the New Jerusalem (1983)

source_context.title: Malcolm Chase on Dorothy Thompson’s historical work

verification.note: Talk checked for the 1976 essay in The Rights and Wrongs of Women, the 1984 Chartists monograph, and her critical engagement with Marxism and feminism. Retrospective scholarly interpretation is distinguished from Thompson’s own interview. Further selected passages checked on The Early Chartists (1971), Queen Victoria (1990), O’Connor’s leadership and Dorothy’s criticism of Saville’s account of Chartism’s decline. Chase explicitly differs over Saville; claims of priority or settled consensus are not adopted as universal verdicts.

source_context.title: Sheila Rowbotham, Hidden from History (Pluto Press, 1973).

verification.note: Author’s university research record checked for title, publisher and 1973 publication. Full text unread; the separate Workshop archive account supports her organizing context.

source_context.title: History Workshop, “The History Workshop Archives: An Introduction” and “History Workshop 4”; Luke Parks, “The History Workshop Archives” (2012; updated 2023).

verification.note: Institutional archive introduction and https://www.historyworkshop.org.uk/public-history/history-workshop-4/ checked: Ruskin participation, the 1969 women’s-history dispute, the 1970 women’s liberation conference, and later itinerant workshops. Parks’s custodial account at https://www.historyworkshop.org.uk/museums-archives-heritage/the-history-workshop-archives/ distinguishes workshop papers/recordings, Samuel’s collection and journal records. These are retrospective descriptions; original archival items were not inspected.

source_context.title: Barbara Taylor: E. P. Thompson and feminist historical inquiry

verification.note: Taylor’s first-person account checked for building on Thompson in Eve and the New Jerusalem (1983), alongside criticism and his resistance. Retrospective testimony; distinguishes her experience from Scott’s arguments and quotes a 1988 interview.

strand.title: Work and family change
strand.focus: Tilly and Scott question assumptions that women at home were unproductive and that wage work automatically meant emancipation.
strand.works: 1975 joint article; Women, Work, and Family (1978)

source_context.title: Joan W. Scott and Louise A. Tilly, “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 17, no. 1 (1975): 36–64.

verification.note: Publisher-hosted primary opening extract and original issue metadata read. Questions assumptions that domestic women were unproductive or that paid work and emancipation formed one linear sequence. Remainder of article and data unread; online 2009 date is not original publication.

source_context.title: Louise A. Tilly and Joan W. Scott, Women, Work, and Family (1978; revised 1987).

verification.note: Indexed publisher preview copyright confirms 1978 and 1987; indexed 1978 book metadata confirms joint authorship. Direct publisher page returned 403. No full book or three-stage model checked; the separate 1975 article supplies the bounded argument here.

strand.title: Period boundaries and historical explanation
strand.focus: Kelly’s Renaissance question and Lerner’s historical account of patriarchy challenge supposedly timeless or universally progressive narratives.
strand.works: “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977); The Creation of Patriarchy (1986)

source_context.title: Joan Kelly-Gadol, “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” in Becoming Visible: Women in European History (1977).

verification.note: Primary opening pp. 176–177 and note 1 in a later course reprint read; 1977 first publication checked against indexed original metadata. Challenges periodization and Burckhardt’s equality claim while distinguishing social positions and prescribed ideals from practice. Full literary analysis and subsequent debate unread.

source_context.title: Gerda Lerner, The Creation of Patriarchy (Oxford University Press, 1986).

verification.note: Indexed author-site description checked for historical rather than biological explanation of patriarchy in the ancient Near East; direct page returned 403 and displayed edition is 1987. Original 1986 checked in book metadata and Chakravarti’s 1993 bibliography. No full primary monograph or archaeological evidence read.

strand.title: Black women’s historical questions
strand.focus: Slavery, professional institutions, religion and racial analysis are distinct subjects and methods.
strand.works: Black Women in White (1989); Ar’n’t I a Woman? (1985); Righteous Discontent (1993)

source_context.title: Hine: Black Women in White (1989)

verification.note: Author’s Northwestern profile consulted for research in African American women’s history and bibliography, including this 1989 book. No inference that all Black women’s history shares one method.

source_context.title: Deborah Gray White, Ar’n’t I a Woman? Female Slaves in the Plantation South (Norton, 1985); Rutgers interview by Patricia Lamiell.

verification.note: Retrospective interview and introduction checked for the 1985 book and White’s emphasis on enslaved women’s work and reproduction. The site’s apparent default 1969 date contradicts its contents and is not used as an interview date. Full 1985 book and revised edition unread.

source_context.title: Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham, Righteous Discontent: The Women’s Movement in the Black Baptist Church, 1880–1920 (Harvard University Press, 1993).

verification.note: Author’s institutional publication list checked for title, date and subject. No primary chapters read; this record does not verify a detailed interpretation of the politics of respectability. Later coauthored Franklin editions are outside the mapped period.

source_context.title: Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham, “African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race,” Signs 17, no. 2 (Winter 1992): 251–274.

verification.note: Primary opening pp. 251–252 and notes 1–2 read. Higginbotham credits feminist conceptual resources while criticizing inadequate racial analysis; the notes name Scott, Butler and earlier women-of-color scholarship. Remaining examples and later reception have not been checked in full.

strand.title: National and regional syntheses
strand.focus: French collaborative synthesis, German social history and Nigerian women’s history have different scopes and documentary bases.
strand.works: Histoire des femmes, vol. 4 (1991); Women in German History (1989 English); Nigerian Women (1992)

source_context.title: Geneviève Fraisse and Michelle Perrot, editors, Histoire des femmes en Occident, vol. 4: Le XIXe siècle (Plon, 1991), series directed by Georges Duby and Michelle Perrot.

verification.note: Indexed BnF catalogue confirms the 1991 volume, volume editors and series directors; direct encoded URL failed. No introduction or essays read. This is a collaborative French-language synthesis with Western scope, not evidence of one common theory.

source_context.title: Ute Frevert, Women in German History: From Bourgeois Emancipation to Sexual Liberation (Berg, 1989; linked paperback 1990).

verification.note: Publisher contents checked for bourgeois society, gender, rights/duties and changing opportunities/restrictions through 1988. Åbo Akademi catalogue https://www.finna.fi/Record/abo.99274683405972 corroborates 1989 English publication. Institutional profile https://www.mpib-berlin.mpg.de/staff/ute-frevert records Bielefeld habilitation in 1989 and lists this work. Institutional connection supports a contextual contributor, not adherence to every Sonderweg thesis. No full book or claim that this work alone transformed the school.

source_context.title: Bolanle Awe, ed., Nigerian Women in Historical Perspective (Sankore, 1992).

verification.note: National Library of Nigeria repository contents, 1992 metadata and reproduced account of the collection’s publication difficulties checked. Essays address multiple women and settings. The linked PDF did not open through the web tool; no individual essay read, and listed women are not automatically classified as historians.

strand.title: Life histories and written lives
strand.focus: Davis, Bozzoli/Nkotsoe and Kaplan use different personal evidence; no single life stands for all women.
strand.works: Women on the Margins (1995); Women of Phokeng (1991); Between Dignity and Despair (1998)

source_context.title: Natalie Zemon Davis, Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (Harvard University Press, 1995).

verification.note: Indexed Folger catalogue description consulted for three differently situated women and their surviving writings; original 1995 distinguished from 1997 electronic record. Direct page failed. No full chapters or source reconstructions checked.

source_context.title: Belinda Bozzoli with the assistance of Mmantho Nkotsoe, Women of Phokeng: Consciousness, Life Strategy, and Migrancy in South Africa, 1900–1983 (1991).

verification.note: University-hosted primary cover and introduction scan, printed pp. 1–7, visually read. Author credit retains “with the assistance of”; p. 6 identifies Nkotsoe as interviewer and describes the jointly conceived twenty-two-life-history project. Supports migration, gender, material conditions and interpreted consciousness rather than unmediated experience. Publisher indexed listing and contemporary Cambridge review metadata corroborate 1991; full case chapters unread.

source_context.title: Marion A. Kaplan, Between Dignity and Despair: Jewish Life in Nazi Germany (Oxford University Press, 1998).

verification.note: Publisher abstract checked for memoirs, diaries, interviews and letters, families and women’s experience, and the limits of hindsight about emigration and persecution. The online edition is 1999; Wiener Holocaust Library catalogue https://wiener.soutron.net/Portal/Default/en-GB/OpenedRecords/OpenSelected/24768 confirms original 1998. Full chapters unread; publisher priority claims are not adopted.

strand.title: Caste and historical patriarchy
strand.focus: Chakravarti examines upper-caste sexual control and social hierarchy through early Indian texts. Prescriptions must be distinguished from lived practices.

source_context.title: Uma Chakravarti, “Conceptualising Brahmanical Patriarchy in Early India: Gender, Caste, Class and State,” Economic and Political Weekly 28, no. 14 (3 April 1993): 579–585.

verification.note: Primary opening p. 579 and Lerner bibliography entry read. Explicitly uses Lerner’s historical approach while investigating caste and sexual control in early India. Brahmanical prescriptions are not direct descriptions of all women’s lives; later sections, textual evidence and reception remain unchecked.

strand.title: Medieval women, rules and recorded practice
strand.focus: Power examines the production and survival of visitation evidence and warns against equating a catalogue of faults with the whole life of a community. Her confidence in truthful findings remains an argument to test.

source_context.title: Eileen Power: Medieval English Nunneries

verification.note: Primary text at https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/39537/pg39537-images.html : complete general and author’s prefaces, selected opening pp. 1–3 and complete pp. 493–498 read. General preface belongs to G. G. Coulton, not Power. Author credits Hamilton Thompson’s transcripts, translations and reading; excludes Gilbertine houses and Henry VIII commissioners’ testimony for specified reasons. Discussion differentiates visitation findings from injunctions and warns that fault-seeking records are incomplete. Her stronger assertions of their truth and representativeness are not independently endorsed. Main cases, notes and registers unread. Previous scope: Cambridge publisher listing identifies the 1922 original and its study of medieval nunneries. Digital publication and reissue dates are later; the whole book has not been audited.

strand.title: Collecting records, access and unequal authority
strand.focus: Preserving documents, making them discoverable and bringing them into teaching involve collective labor. WCWA’s broadened mission and Black women’s limited authority/funding complicate an uncomplicated recovery narrative.
strand.works: WCWA and Smith collecting; Voss-Hubbard (1995); Cott, ed., A Woman Making History (1991)

source_context.title: Anke Voss-Hubbard, “No Documents—No History”: Mary Ritter Beard and the Early History of Women’s Archives, American Archivist 58/1 (Winter 1995), pp. 16–30.

verification.note: Complete article read, including separately recovered pp. 21–22 and 26–27. Uses correspondence, annual reports and Grierson interviews to reconstruct WCWA and Smith collecting, cataloguing, teaching and donor work. Documents Black women’s marginal authority/funding and organizational disputes alongside achievements. Original letters/reports and Collier-Thomas’s cited 1986 essay are mediated, not independently read. No sole-founder claim or universal claim about women’s archives is adopted.

source_context.title: Nancy F. Cott, ed., A Woman Making History: Mary Ritter Beard Through Her Letters (Yale University Press, 1991).

verification.note: Publisher description and publication metadata checked. Documents a collection of 141 letters and Cott’s recovery of correspondence from recipients’ archives. Letters and introductory essay not independently read; promotional founding claims not adopted. This supports editorial recovery, not a particular interpretation attributed to an unread letter.

strand.title: Southern women: documentary scope and later reissues
strand.focus: Spruill distinguishes domestic institutions, public activity and status. Scott’s reissues renew access; Richter values the book while questioning its limited inquiry into Black and Native women.
strand.works: Women’s Life and Work (1938; reissues 1972, 1998); Richter review (1999)

source_context.title: Julie Richter, review of Julia Cherry Spruill, Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies, H-SAWH, March 1999.

verification.note: Complete review read from original H-Net HTML obtained with curl after browser access failed. Quotes Spruill’s original preface and p. 208, describes Scott’s reissue introduction, and documents Colonial Williamsburg use. Criticism concerns questions not asked about Black and Native women, not their total absence. Richter’s planned use for a slavery study is future intent. Book, original preface and Scott introductions remain mediated; friendship with Beard does not establish methodological transmission.

source_context.title: Anne Firor Scott, ed., Unheard Voices: The First Historians of Southern Women (University Press of Virginia, 1993).

verification.note: Smithsonian Libraries catalogue checks 1993 date, editor and contents, including Spruill’s “Conjugal felicity” and domestic discord. Richter’s 1999 review separately cites the volume. Full introduction and collected texts unread; contents do not establish agreement among contributors.

strand.title: Rights movements, archival reach and historical boundaries
strand.focus: Flexner’s labor and Black women’s coverage broadens a suffrage narrative. Rupp distinguishes participants’ self-definition from historians’ expanded categories; James asks a different question about structural explanation.
strand.works: Century of Struggle (1959); James (1960) and Rupp (1992) reception

source_context.title: Frances James, “Century of Women’s Struggle,” International Socialist Review 21/1 (Winter 1960), pp. 27–28.

verification.note: Complete contemporary review read. Welcomes labor and Black women’s coverage but criticizes the absence of a private-property explanation and program beyond reform. These are James’s judgments. Quoted preface remains mediated; the review’s Sojourner Truth speech version is not treated as a verified transcript. Frances James is not conflated with Janet Wilson James.

source_context.title: Leila J. Rupp, “Eleanor Flexner’s Century of Struggle: Women’s History and the Women’s Movement,” NWSA Journal 4/2 (Summer 1992), pp. 157–169.

verification.note: Partial public article preview consulted: pp. 157, 159–160, 162–163, 165–166 and 168–169; pp. 158, 161, 164 and 167 are absent. JSTOR stable ID 4316194. Available passages support archival resources, race/class coverage and movement-boundary debate. Original Flexner bibliography, Catt–Conrad letters and Rivers review remain mediated. Papers’ closure described in 1992 is not a current access claim; omitted text is not inferred.
